questions.stem: Name the tense of the verb in the sentence "Adaeze has been reading since four o'clock."
questions.explanation: The pattern *has/have + been + -ing* is the present perfect continuous. It shows an action that began in the past and is still going on, which is exactly why *since four o'clock* fits. Had the sentence read *had been reading*, the tense would have shifted to past perfect continuous.

distractorRationale.a: Present continuous is *is reading*, with no *has been*
distractorRationale.b: Present perfect is *has read*, without the -ing form
distractorRationale.d: Past perfect continuous uses *had been*, not *has been*

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "I ______ the new principal at the staff meeting last Tuesday."
questions.explanation: *Last Tuesday* names a finished point in past time, and finished past time takes the simple past. The present perfect is used only when the time is unspecified or the period is still open, as in "I have met her twice this term".

distractorRationale.a: The present perfect cannot appear with a finished time expression such as *last Tuesday*
distractorRationale.c: The past perfect needs a second, later past event to be earlier than
distractorRationale.d: The continuous form suggests a repeated or ongoing meeting, which does not fit a single occasion

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "By the time we reached the park, the last bus to Onitsha ______."
questions.explanation: Two past events are involved, and the departure happened before the arrival. The past perfect, *had left*, is the tense that marks the earlier of two past actions, while the simple past *reached* marks the later one.

distractorRationale.a: Mixes present perfect with a clearly past main clause
distractorRationale.b: The simple past would place both events at the same time and lose the sequence
distractorRationale.d: The past continuous would mean the bus was in the act of departing as they arrived, a different meaning

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "My uncle ______ in Kano since 2015."
questions.explanation: *Since* marks a starting point in the past for a situation that still continues, and that combination requires the present perfect. The sentence means he moved there in 2015 and is there now, which the simple present alone cannot express.

distractorRationale.a: The simple present states a habit but cannot reach back to 2015
distractorRationale.b: The simple past would imply that he no longer lives in Kano
distractorRationale.d: The present continuous suggests a temporary arrangement and does not combine with *since 2015*

questions.stem: Name the tense of the verb in the sentence "By December the contractor will have completed the classroom block."
questions.explanation: The pattern *will have + past participle* is the future perfect, used for an action that will be finished before a stated future time. *By December* is exactly the kind of deadline expression that calls for it.

distractorRationale.a: Simple future would be *will complete*, with no sense of a deadline already passed
distractorRationale.b: Future continuous would be *will be completing*, stressing the action in progress
distractorRationale.d: Present perfect is *has completed* and refers to the present, not the future

questions.stem: Report this statement correctly: Musa said, "I am writing my project report."

options.text: Musa said that he is writing his project report.
Musa said that he was writing his project report.
Musa said that he has been writing his project report.
Musa said that he will write his project report.

questions.explanation: When the reporting verb is in the past — *said* — the tense of the reported words shifts one step back. Present continuous *am writing* therefore becomes past continuous *was writing*, and the pronoun *I* becomes *he*.

distractorRationale.a: Leaves the reported verb in the present, so the tense does not follow the past reporting verb
distractorRationale.c: Changes the meaning to a stretch of activity rather than what he was doing at the time of speaking
distractorRationale.d: Turns a statement about the present into a promise about the future

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences keeps its tenses consistent?

options.text: She opened the door, walks into the room and sat down.
She opened the door, walked into the room and sat down.
She opens the door, walked into the room and sits down.
She opened the door, walks into the room and sits down.

questions.explanation: When several actions happen in the same time frame, all the verbs must stay in the same tense. Option b keeps all three in the simple past. Unmotivated shifting between past and present is one of the commonest faults penalised in the essay paper.

distractorRationale.a: Shifts from past to present and back again in one sentence
distractorRationale.c: Shifts twice, giving no consistent time frame at all
distractorRationale.d: Starts in the past and finishes in the present with no reason for the change

questions.stem: The present perfect tense may be used with a finished time expression such as *yesterday*.
questions.explanation: False. The present perfect links the past to now, so it cannot be pinned to a time that is over. "I have seen him yesterday" is wrong; write "I saw him yesterday" with the simple past, or "I have seen him today" where the period is still open.

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "If I ______ enough money now, I would buy the recommended textbooks."
questions.explanation: The main clause uses *would buy*, which marks this as a second conditional — an imagined present situation that is contrary to fact. The *if* clause of a second conditional takes the simple past form, so *had* is required even though the time referred to is the present.

distractorRationale.a: *Have* would produce a first conditional, which needs *will buy* in the main clause
distractorRationale.c: *Will* never appears in the *if* clause of a conditional sentence
distractorRationale.d: *Would have* belongs to the third conditional, which refers to an unreal past

questions.stem: Choose the option that completes the sentence correctly: "The class teacher told us that she ______ our scripts before the holiday began."
questions.explanation: The reporting verb *told* is past, so the reported verb must shift back, and the marking also happened before the holiday began — an event already in the past. Both requirements point to the past perfect *had marked*.

distractorRationale.a: Leaves the verb in the present after a past reporting verb
distractorRationale.b: Present perfect does not backshift correctly after *told*
distractorRationale.d: *Will* refers forward, contradicting *before the holiday began*
